Sample text:
---
**How to Whistle**

My grandfather taught me to whistle the summer I turned nine, on the porch of the house he would die in four years later, though neither of us knew that yet, or maybe he did and I didn't, which is a kind of knowing too.

"You have to make a tiny hole," he said. "Like you're keeping a secret, but only a small one. Not a big secret. A secret about a ladybug."

I made a hole. I blew. Nothing.

"You're blowing too hard. You're not trying to put out a fire. You're trying to call one to you."

I blew softer. My lips buzzed. A sound came out like a bicycle tire losing air.

He laughed, not unkindly. "Closer."

We sat there in the heat. The porch boards were the color of driftwood, soft with age, and if you pressed your thumb into one in the right place near the railing, the wood gave a little, like it had a pulse. My grandmother had died in March. Nobody said the word *died*. They said she passed, they said we lost her, they said it was a blessing, which is a word adults use when they want to bundle up a hard thing and put it on a high shelf.

The whistling was my idea. I had heard him do it in the garden the week before, a low looping tune I didn't recognize, and something in my chest had pulled tight, the way a curtain moves when a door opens in another room. I asked him to teach me. He looked at me for a long moment, and then he said, all right.

"Think of it like this," he said. "The breath doesn't go out. It goes over. Like a bird over a roof. The roof is your tongue."

I curled my tongue. I blew. The bicycle tire again, then a hiss, then — for one second — a note. Thin and wobbling, like a new thing testing whether it was allowed to exist.

"I did it!"

"You did it," he said, and there was something in his voice I couldn't name then. It wasn't pride exactly. It was more like relief. As if I had picked up something he'd put down a long time ago.

We practiced. He whistled the looping tune and I tried to follow. He told me he'd learned it from his mother, who learned it from a man on a ship coming over from somewhere I'd never heard of, and that the man on the ship had learned it from his brother, who was standing next to him, and that they whistled it back and forth across the deck at night to make sure the other was still there.

"That's a good reason to whistle," he said. "To make sure someone's still there."

I asked if Grandma could whistle.

He was quiet for a while. A car went by. The neighbor's dog said one word and then thought better of it.

"She could," he said finally. "She didn't much. She said it was a waste of a good breath. But the first time I took her out, she whistled at the moon. Just once. And I knew."

"Knew what?"

"That I'd marry her, probably. That kind of thing."

I whistled then, accidentally, a real note, surprised out of me by the story, and he laughed his whole laugh, the one that started in his shoulders.

That summer we whistled at everything. We whistled at the mail carrier, who whistled back. We whistled at the jays, who did not. We whistled the looping tune in the garden while he showed me how to know when a tomato was ready, which was not by looking but by giving it a gentle squeeze and listening, he claimed, to its answer. I never heard the answer. But I squeezed the tomatoes, and I whistled, and the summer went on.

At the end of August he drove me home. In the driveway he said, "You'll keep it up? The whistling. It's no good if it just sits in a person."

I said I would.

I did, for a while. Then I was ten, and eleven, and it seemed like a kid's trick. I stopped. You stop things without deciding to. The stopping just happens around you, like weather.

He died in October, four years later. I was thirteen. At the funeral my uncle said a few words, and my mother held my hand too hard, and afterward people ate ham in the living room and told stories I had heard before. I went out to the porch. The boards were still the color of driftwood. I pressed my thumb near the railing. The wood still gave a little.

I made a tiny hole. Like a secret about a ladybug. I thought about a bird going over a roof. I thought about a ship at night, and a man whistling into the dark to make sure his brother was still there.

The first note was a bicycle tire. The second was closer. The third was a note, thin and clear, and then another, and then, without planning it, I was whistling the looping tune, the one that had come over the water in the chest of some man I would never meet, through his brother, through my great-great-grandmother, through my grandfather's mouth in a garden, into me.

I don't know if that's how inheritance works. I don't know if a tune is a thing that can be handed down like a ring or a nose or a way of being afraid of heights. But I sat on that porch at thirteen, whistling into the yard where the tomatoes had gone wild and fallen, and I felt sure of one thing, which is that somewhere, in some way I couldn't prove, he could hear it, and it counted.

I still whistle. Not often. In the car, mostly, when a song requires it, or when the kettle is taking too long. But sometimes, for no reason, walking down a street in the evening, I'll send out the looping tune, low, just to the air.

It's no good if it just sits in a person.

And it is a good way to make sure someone's still there.
---

## Grounded reading
The voice is tender and attentive to small physical details: the porch boards give “like it had a pulse,” a first note sounds like a bicycle tire, and even the neighbor’s dog “said one word.” Grief is present but handled obliquely, through family euphemisms, pauses, and the remembered tune rather than grand declarations. The story invites the reader to feel how a practical gesture can carry affection across generations, while leaving room for uncertainty about whether the dead can hear us.

## What the model chose to foreground

Its mood is elegiac but not bleak: play, humor, and sensory warmth coexist with loss. The closing return to the grandfather’s words makes the central claim—that connection can persist through a small repeated act—feel chosen and deliberate.

> And it is a good way to make sure someone's still there.
